title: Killing them with kindness
intro: A short magazine-style article about why so many houseplants die and how to keep yours alive. Tomasz is a made-up example, not a real person; the article was written for Psotek English
paras: When Tomasz moved into his first flat, he bought six plants to make it feel like home. Within two months, all six were dead. "I watered them every single day," he says. "Nobody could say I didn't care." That, it turns out, was exactly the problem. His story is very common: experts say that more houseplants die from too much attention than from too little.

The biggest killer of indoor plants is overwatering. Roots need air as well as water, and when the soil stays wet for too long, they cannot breathe. Slowly they begin to rot, and the leaves above them turn yellow and droopy. Unfortunately, a thirsty plant and a drowning plant can look almost the same, so many owners react to the warning signs by reaching for the watering can again.

Instead of following a fixed timetable, gardeners recommend a simple test. Push a finger into the soil up to the second knuckle. If it feels dry, water the plant thoroughly, until water runs out of the hole at the bottom of the pot. If it still feels damp, leave it alone and check again in a few days. A pot without a drainage hole is a trap, because the extra water has nowhere to go.

Light is the other half of the story. Every plant comes from a particular natural home, and it does best when you copy those conditions. A cactus from the desert will be happy on a sunny windowsill, while many popular leafy plants come from the shady floor of tropical forests and can burn in strong, direct sun. Before you buy a plant, it is worth reading the small label in the pot rather than choosing it only because it looks pretty.

Last spring, Tomasz decided to give plants another chance. This time he chose just two easy species, put them near a bright window and felt the soil once a week before deciding whether to water. Both are still alive, and one has even produced three new leaves. "I learned that looking after something sometimes means doing less," he says. "Now I wait until they actually need me."

levels.title: Grandma's soup lessons
levels.intro: An easy story about a young man who learns to cook from his grandmother. Piotr and his grandmother are made-up people; the text was written for Psotek English
paras: Until last year, Piotr couldn't cook at all. He was twenty-four and lived alone, but he usually ate sandwiches or ordered pizza. "I was too busy to cook," he says. "And I didn't know where to start."

Everything changed when his grandmother broke her arm. She couldn't use the kitchen for six weeks, so Piotr visited her every Saturday to make lunch. She sat on a chair and told him what to do, step by step.

The first week was a disaster. He cut the vegetables too big, put in too much salt and forgot the soup on the cooker. It burned, and the whole flat smelled terrible. His grandmother laughed and said, "Don't worry. Everybody burns their first soup."

Slowly, Piotr got better. He learned to make chicken soup, potato pancakes and a simple apple cake. He started writing his grandmother's recipes in a notebook, because she never used exact amounts. She always said, "Just a little bit," or "Until it looks right."
Now his grandmother's arm is fine, but Piotr still goes to her flat every Saturday. These days, they cook together. "I come for the food," he says with a smile, "but really, I come for the stories."

levels.title: Tomorrow, definitely
levels.intro: A magazine-style article about why we put things off and what actually helps. Ioana is a made-up example, not a real person; the article was written for Psotek English
paras: Ioana, a graphic designer from Cluj, had a tax form to fill in. It would have taken her forty minutes. Instead, it sat on her desk for five weeks, while she reorganised her bookshelves, cleaned the oven and learned to make sourdough bread. "I was incredibly productive," she jokes. "Just not at the one thing I actually had to do." Most of us will recognise the pattern. Procrastination is not the same as laziness: people who put things off are often extremely busy. They are simply busy with something else.

Psychologists increasingly describe procrastination as a problem of emotions rather than time management. We delay tasks that make us feel bad: bored, anxious, confused or afraid of failing. Putting the task off brings instant relief, and our brains reward us for it, which makes us more likely to do the same thing next time. The cost, of course, arrives later, usually in the form of stress, rushed work and a guilty conscience.

This explains why the classic advice, "Just be more disciplined," rarely works. If the real issue is an unpleasant feeling, then a stricter timetable only adds pressure. What tends to help instead is making the first step so small that it no longer triggers the feeling. Rather than "write the report", the task becomes "open the document and write one sentence". Once people have started, they frequently carry on, partly because unfinished tasks tend to stay on our minds until we complete them.

Another useful technique is to be kinder to yourself. It sounds counterintuitive, but research on students suggests that those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next. Harsh self-criticism, it seems, makes the task feel even more threatening, and so the cycle continues. Changing your surroundings can also make a difference: leaving your phone in another room removes the easiest escape route.

In the end, Ioana finished her tax form on a Sunday morning, in a café, with her phone switched off. It took thirty-five minutes. "The worst part was the five weeks of thinking about it," she admits. She now has a rule: if something will take less than ten minutes, she does it immediately. For bigger jobs, she promises herself just a quarter of an hour. "Usually I keep going. And if I don't, at least I've started."

levels.title: In defence of boredom
levels.intro: An opinion piece arguing that boredom is useful, and that we may have lost something by filling every empty moment. Marek is a made-up example, not a real person; the article was written for Psotek English
paras: When did you last feel genuinely bored? Not restless, not tired, but properly, achingly bored, with nothing to look at and nowhere to be? For many of us, the honest answer is that we can no longer remember. The queue at the post office, the wait for a bus, the five minutes before a meeting starts: every gap in the day is now instantly filled by a screen. Boredom, once an unavoidable part of life, has become something we can switch off at will. It is worth asking whether that is entirely a good thing.

For most of history, boredom has had a bad reputation. Philosophers treated it as a kind of spiritual emptiness; parents and teachers saw it as the first step towards mischief. Yet a growing number of researchers argue that it serves a purpose. Boredom, in their view, is a signal rather than a malfunction. It tells us that what we are doing is not meaningful enough and nudges us to look for something better. Like hunger or pain, it is unpleasant precisely because it is meant to make us act.

The trouble is that we have learned to answer the signal in the laziest possible way. Instead of changing direction, we reach for the nearest source of easy stimulation, which silences the feeling without addressing its cause. The result is a strange combination of constant entertainment and a vague sense of dissatisfaction. We are rarely bored, but we are not necessarily engaged either.

There is also some evidence that letting the mind wander has creative benefits. In one frequently cited type of experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately dull task, such as copying numbers from a phone book, later came up with more ideas in a creativity test than those who went straight to it. The findings are not conclusive, and the effect is probably modest. Still, they fit with what many writers and inventors have long claimed: that their best ideas tend to arrive in the shower, on a walk, or while staring out of a train window, rather than at the desk.

None of this means we should romanticise tedium or throw away our phones. Some boredom is simply a waste of time, and modern technology has brought enormous benefits. But it might be worth reclaiming a few empty moments on purpose. Marek, an engineer who started leaving his phone in his bag during his daily commute, describes the first week as "mildly torturous". By the third, he had sketched out a plan for a side project he had been postponing for years. "I didn't need more time," he says. "I needed fewer distractions in the time I already had."

levels.title: The quiet etiquette of the queue
levels.intro: An essay on what waiting in line reveals about fairness, patience and the unwritten rules we all obey. Helen is a made-up example, not a real person; the essay was written for Psotek English
paras: Few social institutions are as mundane, or as fiercely defended, as the queue. Nobody votes on it, no law spells it out in detail, and yet try stepping in front of a dozen strangers at a ticket office and you will discover just how seriously it is taken. The reaction is rarely violent; it is usually something subtler and, in its way, more devastating: a collective intake of breath, a pointed cough, a remark delivered to no one in particular but clearly intended for you. The queue, it turns out, is a miniature legal system that runs almost entirely on shared assumptions.

At its heart lies a deceptively simple principle: first come, first served. What makes it so robust is not that it is efficient (it often isn't) but that it is transparent. Everyone can see where they stand, literally and figuratively, and everyone can verify that the rule is being applied. Researchers who study waiting have repeatedly found that people care less about how long they wait than about whether the wait is fair. A long line that moves in strict order is tolerated; a shorter one in which others appear to jump ahead provokes disproportionate fury.

This obsession with fairness explains some otherwise puzzling behaviour. Supermarkets that switch from several separate lines to a single, snaking queue feeding multiple tills often find that customers prefer it, even when the average waiting time barely changes. The single line removes the nagging suspicion that you have, once again, chosen the slowest checkout. Similarly, waiting feels noticeably shorter when people can see progress being made, or when they are given a reasonably accurate estimate. Uncertainty, not delay, is what grates.

Yet the queue is also more elastic than its reputation suggests. Most of us accept a whole repertoire of unwritten exceptions: the person with a single item allowed to go ahead, the friend who "was holding a place", the elderly neighbour waved through out of courtesy. These concessions are negotiated wordlessly and on the spot, and they are tolerated only as long as they remain modest. Push them too far, and the goodwill that sustains the system evaporates in seconds.

Helen, who spent a decade managing the box office of a provincial theatre, puts it more bluntly. "People will forgive almost anything: a broken card machine, a sold-out show, the rain. What they won't forgive is the sense that someone else is getting away with something." There is a lesson here that extends well beyond the ticket window. Institutions, from hospitals to governments, are judged not only on the results they deliver but on whether the process looks even-handed. The humble queue, in other words, is a daily rehearsal for a much larger argument about what we owe one another.
